full_description: Scratch makes programming approachable through colourful drag-and-drop coding blocks. child_safety_policy.heading: Creative Coding With Privacy and Parent Supervision.
child_safety_policy.approved_copy: Children can learn Scratch through supervised or offline projects without being required to create public profiles or publish their work. Project reviews and parent showcases are private by default.
safeguards: Public Scratch account creation is optional—never required for grading or certification.
Offline learning fully supported via the official Scratch App for Windows, macOS, ChromeOS, and Android.
Projects are submitted and evaluated privately as local .sb3 files under teacher supervision.
Parent showcase is conducted privately by default with no public video or gallery sharing.
Zero collection or display of children's sensitive personal information (full names, photos, addresses, school details).
Full alignment with Scratch's under-16 parental permission and community guidelines.

online_vs_offline_learning.heading: Code Online or Offline — No Public Profile Required.
online_vs_offline_learning.online_editor: Scratch Web Editor (scratch.mit.edu) accessible through modern browsers for interactive visual coding.
online_vs_offline_learning.offline_app: Official Scratch App (scratch.mit.edu/download) allowing complete offline coding, saving local .sb3 files, and practicing without an internet connection.
online_vs_offline_learning.device_recommendation: A desktop computer or laptop with mouse and keyboard access is strongly recommended for comfortable block drag-and-drop and game control testing.

debugging_computational_thinking.heading: Learning to Fix a Bug Is Part of Learning to Code.
debugging_computational_thinking.workflow: What should happen? → What happened? → Which blocks control it? → What can I change? → Does it work now?
core_concepts: Decomposition: Breaking down game ideas into characters, backdrops, and rules.
Algorithms & Sequencing: Arranging instructions in precise order to achieve the desired action.
Loops & Conditions: Repeating actions and making decisions based on player inputs or collision sensors.
Debugging: Testing programs, identifying discrepancies, and testing corrections systematically.

parent_showcase_model.heading: See What Your Child Created — in a Private Project Showcase.
parent_showcase_model.approved_copy: At the end of the course, children demonstrate their Scratch creations, explain basic coding decisions and share what they learned through a supervised, private parent showcase.
showcase_elements: Demonstrating the playable capstone game and animated story
Explaining how player controls, score variables, and rules function
Sharing one bug they encountered and how they fixed it
Showing how they improved their game based on classmate playtesting feedback

Paper flowcharts and storyboard planning templates

portfolio.title: Scratch Creative Coding & Game Creation Portfolio
portfolio.description: An age-appropriate, hands-on digital coding portfolio demonstrating foundational computational thinking, visual storytelling, game mechanics, debugging, and independent project refinement across three distinct Scratch projects.

deliverables.name: Project 01: Original Animated Story
deliverables.description: Demonstrates sequencing, events, motion, costumes, backdrops, and character dialogue in a creative interactive narrative.
required_elements: Original story with clear beginning, middle, and ending
At least two interacting characters with synchronized dialogue
Costume animation (e.g. walking, expression changes) and backdrop transitions
Event triggers (Green Flag clicked, sprite clicked, or key pressed)
Sound effects timed to dialogue and movement
Viewer interaction and clear conclusion

deliverables.name: Project 02: Functional Scratch Mini-Game
deliverables.description: Demonstrates core game logic including loops, conditions, sensing, collision detection, player controls, and progress tracking.
required_elements: Clear player objective (e.g. maze escape, catching items, obstacle avoidance)
Responsive keyboard or mouse player controls
Repeat and forever loops managing continuous game actions
If/then conditions detecting sprite collisions or boundaries
Score, item collection, or progress counter
Clear win and lose/end game states with reset logic
evidence: Game rules and player instructions card
Debugging note documenting at least one solved issue

deliverables.name: Project 03: Independently Improved Capstone Game
deliverables.type: Original Capstone Game with Iterative Improvements
deliverables.description: An independently planned, tested, and playtested Scratch game demonstrating game mechanics, variables, debugging, peer feedback, and feedback-based improvements.
required_elements: Independent game design storyboard and planning sheet
Playable game mechanics combining loops, conditions, sensing, and variables
Variables for score, lives, or countdown timers
Broadcast messages coordinating stage transitions (start screen, play, win, game-over)
Documented playtest with peer feedback
Meaningful feedback-based improvement (e.g. new level, refined difficulty, revised controls)
Child-friendly verbal explanation of key coding blocks
Private parent demonstration
evidence: Initial game planning sheet and paper storyboard
Draft and final improved Scratch project files (.sb3)

assessment_model.title: Scratch Practical Assessment Rubric
criteria: Navigating the Scratch editor, stage, sprites, backdrops, and costumes
Sequencing blocks logically and breaking tasks into clear steps
Effective use of event triggers (Green Flag, keys, clicks, broadcasts)
Correct application of loops (repeat, forever) and conditions (if/then, if/else)
Sensing and collision detection accuracy in gameplay
Proper setup and resetting of variables (scores, lives, timers)
Playable game controls, clear instructions, and fair challenge design
Independent problem-solving: identifying bugs and testing fixes
Playtesting, listening to peer feedback, and making purposeful improvements
Child-friendly ability to explain what specific code blocks do and why
unacceptable_criteria: Standardized IQ or psychological intelligence tests
Measuring typing speed or raw code volume
Public Scratch followers, likes, comments, or studio popularity
Commercial monetization or professional game development standards
Mandatory public profile creation or compulsory community posting
Penalizing children for encountering normal coding mistakes during learning

modules.title: Creative Coding Foundations
modules.objective: Understand the Scratch environment and learn how simple instructions control characters and actions.

lessons.title: Backdrops
topics: Matching a background to a story.

modules.handsOnLab:
Create a short Scratch scene where a character:

1. Appears on a backdrop.
2. Moves.
3. Changes costume.
4. Says a message.
5. Completes a short action sequence.

### Unplugged Activity

Use paper arrows to plan a simple character journey.
modules.assignment: Create a short interactive greeting or movement scene demonstrating sequencing and at least one event.
modules.deliverable:
**Scratch Coding Foundations Practice Project**

This is a module exercise, not one of the three required major portfolio projects.
modules.assessmentCriteria:
Check whether the child can:

- Identify basic editor areas.
- Connect blocks.
- Predict actions.
- Explain instruction order.
- Save a project.

---

modules.title: Interactive Stories & Animation
modules.objective: Use Scratch to create an original animated story with characters, dialogue, movement and interactive events.
modules.handsOnLab: Create a short interactive animated story involving at least two characters.
modules.assignment:
Complete the first major portfolio project.

## PROJECT 01 — ORIGINAL ANIMATED STORY

Required:

- Original story.
- At least two characters.
- Multiple events.
- Meaningful sequence.
- At least one backdrop or costume change.
- Simple dialogue.
- Some viewer interaction.
- Working ending or clear conclusion.
modules.assessmentCriteria:
Check:

- Originality.
- Sequencing.
- Event use.
- Visual consistency.
- Clarity.
- Functionality.
- Ability to explain blocks.
modules.importantRule:
Do not require public online sharing.

Accept an `.sb3` file or an appropriate private teacher-reviewed project demonstration.

---

modules.title: Game Mechanics & Problem-Solving
modules.objective: Build a functional beginner game using loops, conditions, sensing, player controls and debugging.
modules.handsOnLab:
Build a playable game featuring:

- Player input.
- Repetition.
- Rules.
- Collision detection.
- Score or progress.
- Win or lose condition.
modules.assignment:
Complete the second major portfolio project.

## PROJECT 02 — FUNCTIONAL MINI-GAME

Required:

1. Clear game goal.
2. Working controls.
3. At least one loop.
4. At least one condition.
5. Sensing/collision.
6. A simple progress or scoring system.
7. Clear win or end state.
8. Basic debugging evidence.
modules.assessmentCriteria:
Check:

- Logical rules.
- Playability.
- Functional controls.
- Correct loop usage.
- Appropriate conditions.
- Debugging ability.
- Student explanation.
modules.importantRule:
A copied tutorial without meaningful independent contribution is insufficient evidence of original practical competence.

---

modules.title: Advanced Beginner Scratch
modules.objective: Improve beginner projects using variables, messages, timers and other age-appropriate Scratch game logic.

lessons.title: User Experience for Kids
topics: Can a player understand the goal?

modules.handsOnLab:
Improve a previous game by adding:

- At least one meaningful variable.
- A message/broadcast.
- Clear game state.
- Improved instructions or gameplay.
modules.assignment: Prepare the capstone plan and demonstrate at least one improved game mechanic.
modules.deliverable:
**Advanced Beginner Game Mechanics Exercise & Capstone Planning Sheet**

This supports the final major project rather than counting as an additional independent portfolio game.
modules.assessmentCriteria:
Check:

- Variables.
- Broadcasts.
- Reset behaviour.
- Simple game-state understanding.
- Appropriate code explanations.

---

modules.title: Original Game Capstone
modules.objective: Independently plan, create, test, improve and explain a playable Scratch game.

lessons.title: Child-Friendly Code Explanation
topics: How did you fix a bug?

modules.handsOnLab: Build and test one original capstone game.
modules.assignment:
Complete the third major portfolio project.

## PROJECT 03 — INDEPENDENTLY IMPROVED CAPSTONE GAME

Required:

1. Original or substantially independently developed concept.
2. Planning sheet.
3. Functional controls.
4. At least one loop.
5. At least one meaningful condition.
6. Sensing or collision logic.
7. Score, timer or progress variable.
8. Clear game goal.
9. Working end/restart behaviour.
10. Evidence of debugging.
11. Peer feedback.
12. Meaningful improvement after feedback.
13. Child-friendly explanation.
14. Private parent demonstration.
modules.deliverable: **One Original, Playable and Independently Improved Scratch Game**
modules.importantRule:
Teacher guidance is allowed.

However, the student must be able to explain important choices and demonstrate meaningful independent work.

Do not describe a copied classroom tutorial as an independently invented game.

---

faq.question: What is Scratch Programming & Game Creation?
faq.answer: It is a beginner-friendly course where children learn visual coding through animated stories, games and interactive projects.

faq.question: What is the recommended age?
faq.answer: The course is recommended for children aged 8–12.

faq.question: Does my child need previous coding experience?
faq.answer: No. The course begins with basic visual programming concepts.

faq.question: Does my child need to know Python?
faq.answer: No. Python and other text-based languages are outside this course.

faq.question: How long is the course?
faq.answer: Six weeks with 32 learning hours.

faq.question: What is the fee?
faq.answer: ₹4,900, subject to Nova Skills' verified pricing and tax policy.

faq.question: What is Scratch?
faq.answer: Scratch is a free visual programming environment used to create interactive stories, animations and games.

faq.question: Will my child learn to create games?
faq.answer: Yes. The portfolio includes a functional mini-game and an original capstone game.

faq.question: Will my child create animations?
faq.answer: Yes. The course includes an original animated story project.

faq.question: What coding concepts will be taught?
faq.answer: Sequencing, events, loops, conditions, sensing, variables, broadcasts and debugging.

faq.question: What is block programming?
faq.answer: It is a visual programming approach where learners connect blocks representing instructions.

faq.question: Will my child learn how to fix coding errors?
faq.answer: Yes. Debugging is a core part of the course.

faq.question: Will my child complete original projects?
faq.answer: Yes. Three distinct portfolio projects are required, including independently improved capstone work.

faq.question: Are all students required to create the same game?
faq.answer: No. Students may develop different appropriate game ideas while demonstrating the required concepts.

faq.question: Does Scratch require a paid license?
faq.answer: No. Scratch is free to use.

faq.question: Can Scratch be used offline?
faq.answer: Yes. A Scratch app is available for supported devices.

faq.question: Is a Scratch account compulsory?
faq.answer: No. Children can complete course projects without a public Scratch account.

faq.question: Does my child need to publish projects publicly?
faq.answer: No. Project assessment and parent showcases are private by default.

faq.question: Can children share projects online if parents approve?
faq.answer: Where permitted by Scratch's current account rules, families may voluntarily consider sharing. It is not required for the course.

faq.question: What are Scratch's parental permission rules?
faq.answer: Scratch currently requires parental/guardian permission for new users under 16 to verify accounts for online community participation.

faq.question: What equipment is needed?
faq.answer: A compatible computer with appropriate mouse/keyboard access is recommended. Specific requirements depend on the chosen online or offline setup.

faq.question: Is this course suitable for complete beginners?
faq.answer: Yes. Basic computer familiarity is sufficient.

faq.question: Will parents see the final projects?
faq.answer: The curriculum includes a private parent showcase, subject to the institute's actual delivery arrangements.

faq.question: Will my child receive feedback?
faq.answer: Yes. The course includes teacher feedback, playtesting and project improvements.

faq.question: Will this course improve logical thinking?
faq.answer: It provides structured opportunities to practise sequencing, logical decisions and problem-solving. Individual development varies.

faq.question: Is this professional game development?
faq.answer: No. This is an age-appropriate introduction to visual programming and game logic.

faq.question: Will my child learn AI or Roblox?
faq.answer: No. Those subjects belong to separate, appropriately designed courses.

faq.question: What will the final portfolio contain?
faq.answer: One animated story, one mini-game and one independently improved capstone game.

faq.question: Can children learn without joining the Scratch online community?
faq.answer: Yes. Supervised and offline options support learning without mandatory public community participation.

faq.question: What can my child learn next?
faq.answer: Suitable follow-on options may include Python for Kids, Young Coders Program or other age-appropriate Kids Tech Academy courses, subject to readiness.  ---
